newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: FORECAST-Miserable results seen at Sappi.
newsitem.headline: FORECAST-Miserable results seen at Sappi.

text.p: South African pulp and paper producer Sappi Ltd is seen posting a miserable set of first half results next week as the firm continues to be hamstrung by a hostile price environment, analysts said Friday.
Both in its local market and abroad Sappi is combating low prices that are crimping profits and driving down its attributable earnings.

"It reflects the very, very low prices and difficult trading conditions that they have had. It is really a prices story. Operationally they will have improved," said one analyst who declined to be named.

After a disastrous second half of last year which saw the firm post earnings per share of just 15 cents, few analysts are predicting a substantial improvement in the first half of the current year when it reports figures on Monday.
Forecasts for earnings in the six months to March 31 are in a range of 10 to 40 cents with the consensus figure coming in at 27.5 cents, from 215 cents in the same period last year.
The dividend is at best seen being cut and at worst scrapped. The range was nil to 50 with a consensus figure of 23.3, from 70 cents last time.

The main problem locally is the slow growth of the South African economy, which on Thursday showed a surprise fall in first quarter gross domestic product. That has stymied demand and created a tough market.

"Offshore from a volume perspective they are doing well, but from a margin perspective it is not so good. Customers have high levels of inventory holdings therefore there is a balance of supply and demand that is keeping prices stable at a low level," SocGen Frankel Pollack analyst Mark Rule said.
There have been some hints recently that the bottom has been reached in the prices cycle, offering a tentative hope that the firm will now see prices rise.

On May 20 Finnish forestry group Enso said there had been a clear, though cautious, upturn in pulp prices that could support an uplift in paper prices. On the same day Sweden's AB Kinnevik said pulp inventory holdings were falling, giving scope for pulp increases later in the year.
Most analysts agree that some form of turnaround in the prices cycle is likely by the end of the current year, but to many Sappi still looks a risky investment.

"The question is 'Is Sappi cheap?' and at these levels I don't think it is. But they have bottomed out and if the cycle turns suddenly Sappi could really fly," said one analyst who declined to be named.
Sappi's shares have had a roller-coaster ride so far in 1997, coming off a high of 46.40 rand in early January to hit a low of 32.00 rand in march. They are currently hovering just under 42.00 rand.
